#191689. Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Sources indicate that in the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed.
  • It has been revealed that some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that in the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

It has been revealed that some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

Recent findings suggest that in a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

According to recent reports, at a similar tech giant, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

For some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

According to recent reports, cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might proposal to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

Sources indicate that it works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

“Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

According to recent reports, the Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

Recent findings suggest that at Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The organization also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment plan. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

Sources indicate that there’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

And today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious problem in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Recent findings suggest that your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

Latest Update: What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye.
  • In a recent development, grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

In a recent development, grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” states Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

In a recent development, “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on Tuesday, Nov.
  • Industry observers note that at 5:45 a.m.
  • EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

Industry observers note that at 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, that evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

#191686. Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.
  • Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.
  • Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.

Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.

Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time. This is mainly due to the fact that the same styles of tools and carvings show up across the entire continent. Even so, DNA from Ice Age samples has mostly supported the isolated view.

A woman who died around 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France has changed that.

In a recent development, most of her ancestry came from the western European people of her time. However, part of it also came from populations related to central and eastern Europe. The mixing happened roughly 32,500 to 31,500 years ago.

The analysis of her DNA now gives the oldest set of genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

According to recent reports, pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna‘s Department of Evolutionary Anthropology led the work. Their co-authors include researchers at Harvard Medical School, the University of Cantabria and the University of Upcoming Mexico.

Recent findings suggest that the study rests on DNA from three new Ice Age individuals and one sample of cave sediment. Thus, the picture it draws is built from very few people.

The bone fragment of the woman was recovered from Isturitz Cave in the Basque Country, western Pyrenees. Excavators dug it up in the 1950s, and it stayed in a Paris institute for over 60 years. Then, in 2013, Pinhasi took a sample from it for DNA analysis.

In a recent development, the team recovered more than 454,000 of the genetic markers it was looking for. This represents one of the richest Gravettian datasets yet.

Sources indicate that gravettian is the name for the culture that spread across Europe during the onset of the last Ice Age, between about 34,000 and 25,000 years ago. This culture is known for its shared tool styles, burial practices and portable art.

Until now, DNA data from this Ice Age period in Europe sorted into two stable groups, a western one and a central-eastern one, with little sign of contact between them.

According to recent reports, the Isturitz woman belongs mostly to the western group. But several tests also found a share of her ancestry related to the ancestors of people buried at Dolní Věstonice in what is now the Czech Republic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gelabert remarked the find overturned a long-held assumption.

“Until this newly introduced genomic data, we assumed that the people in Southwestern Europe were quite the same for more than 20,000 years,” he remarked.

The new data, he said, point to population movements that were probably continental in scale, and that the team doesn’t yet clearly understand.

Isturitz is one of the richest Ice Age sites in southern Europe, with an unusual number of carved objects and signs of repeated, intensive occupation.

Sources indicate that archaeologists have long argued that it was a gathering place where different groups met to hunt, trade, socialize and find partners. The cave lies at the natural passage between the rest of Europe and the Iberian Peninsula.

Industry observers note that the woman isn’t alone. When the team reanalyzed a previously published genome from Ormesson, near Paris, dated to about 31,800 to 30,000 years ago, it found a similar eastern signal.

In addition, Belgian individuals from Goyet Cave, about 28,000 to 26,000 years old, were already known to carry mixed ancestry.

Two explanations are possible, the authors wrote. People from the east may have moved west during the Gravettian itself. Or the eastern-looking ancestry may be an older component, already in western Europe before 35,000 years ago.

The team favors the first. The DNA signal is absent from earlier Ice Age genomes in the same region, and it vanishes from southwestern Europe after 30,000 years ago.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team took two pinches of sediment, 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) each.

They came from a layer dated to about 22,100 to 21,700 years ago, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, when human remains are extremely rare. No bone or tooth was needed, only the dirt that people had walked on.

It has been revealed that the researchers built nine DNA libraries from those two extracts and sequenced them 101 times. Out of roughly a billion DNA fragments, more than 294,000 were human.

After the team kept only fragments showing the chemical damage of real ancient DNA, 14,737 genetic markers remained, enough to read the ancestry of the people who used the cave.

The sediment’s ancestry matched the western group, the Isturitz woman’s lineage, so that ancestry persisted in the region through the coldest millennia.

It has been revealed that “Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” Pinhasi said. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”.

According to recent reports, gelabert told Earth.com the team had recovered DNA from this cave’s sediment before. “What surprised us this time is that the quality is unmatched,” he said.

He described the sample as one of the richest sources of human DNA ever reported. For the first time in the region’s Upper Paleolithic, he noted, it let the team tie a culture to a group of people.

The third fresh genome came from Ostuni Cave in southern Italy and belongs to a male fetus about 27,800 to 27,400 years old.

Industry observers note that the team identified him as a first-degree relative of a woman from the same cave whose genome was already published. He was most likely her son.

Comparing the two showed that his father came from the same population as his mother, as far as the data can tell. Yet the parents were not close relatives.

The boy’s genome carried no long stretches of identical DNA from both parents, and the population he came from was genetically larger than any other Gravettian group measured so far.

Gelabert said this is the first mother-and-fetus pair of genomes from the European Paleolithic, and that comparing them is what showed how genetically diverse her population was.

All three individuals, and the people in the El Mirón sediment, are predicted to have had dark skin, dark hair and brown eyes. That was the usual pattern for Europeans of that era.

The whole Gravettian, Solutrean and Epigravettian record, three Ice Age cultures, rests on genome-wide data from fewer than 50 people. This study adds an extra three.

The third is a tooth from Chufín Cave in Cantabria, dated to about 26,000 years ago. It was so degraded that it yielded fewer than 20,000 markers, enough to place it in the western group and little more.

Sediment has its own limits. The DNA in it comes from several people mixed together, and the team’s reading suggests more of them were male than female. The date for the east-west mixing also assumes it happened in a single pulse.

The study does not settle where the eastern ancestry came from. The authors wrote that no particular central European group stands out as the source, and that no genome from the earlier Aurignacian culture exists for southwestern Europe to compare against.

The team did find one thing the data argue against. Earlier work on tooth shapes had suggested a population turnover in western Europe around 28,000 years ago.

The latest genomes, the sediment and the reanalyzed published data instead show the same western ancestry in place from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Gelabert returned to the sediment.

Industry observers note that “Next step is clearly to find out when the population movements that we see in Isturitz really happened. Sediment will be key for this goal,” he said.

The authors named a target: the Aurignacian layers of Isturitz itself, deposits older than the woman, which could show whether the eastern signal was already there before she was born.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#191683. Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1075 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.
  • It has been revealed that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years.
  • It has been revealed that an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.

It has been revealed that air pollution has been linked to dementia for years. It is difficult, however, to work out what happens inside the brain between the time a person breathes in polluted air and the onset of memory problems.

It has been revealed that an experiment in Ohio has provided some clues. After months of breathing polluted air, laboratory mice kept their weight, groomed themselves and went about their usual activities without obvious signs of distress.

Put those same mice in a maze they had already learned to navigate, though, and something was wrong.

Changes had taken place inside their brains, even in animals that had no genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s-like disease.

Before working with mice, the team examined health records from 475,325 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2010.

In a recent development, the median age at enrollment was 58. Over a median follow-up period of nearly 14 years, 12,758 participants developed Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia or died of an Alzheimer’s-related cause.

The researchers wanted to know how much of the risk was associated with where people lived and how much was associated with their genes.

Higher levels of fine particle pollution were linked to dementia, even after accounting for factors such as smoking and diabetes.

People with greater inherited susceptibility also faced higher risk, although the combined association was smaller than expected if the two individual effects multiplied.

For the animal experiments, the team used air collected outdoors in Cleveland, Ohio.

The particles of interest were PM2.5, a group of airborne particles measuring about one ten-thousandth of an inch (2.5 micrometers) or less.

The samples contained a mixture of substances associated with dust and combustion, including iron, nickel and copper.

The team concentrated the particles until their levels reached roughly 10 times those measured outdoors in Cleveland. The resulting concentration was comparable to the average reported for Newly introduced Delhi in 2023.

At just four weeks old, mice began breathing either this polluted air or filtered air for eight hours a day, five days a week. Among them were animals carrying five genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease.

Sixteen weeks into the experiment, the team began testing the animals’ memory.

One test involved a circular platform with an escape hole. Over three days, the mice had repeated opportunities to learn where the hole was, followed by a two-day break before their final test.

Sources indicate that ordinary mice breathing polluted air had about as much difficulty finding the hole as Alzheimer’s-prone mice breathing filtered air. The genetically vulnerable mice exposed to pollution struggled the most.

Other tests revealed problems recognizing unfamiliar objects, weaker muscles in the front and back legs, and behavior consistent with increased anxiety.

Industry observers note that blood vessels in the brain have a protective barrier that limits what can pass from the blood into surrounding brain tissue. Without a properly functioning barrier, potentially harmful substances have easier access to that tissue.

To check for leaks, the team used three chemical markers, including a blue dye.

Much more of these substances escaped from blood vessels in pollution-exposed mice than in ordinary mice breathing filtered air.

Some of the leakage measurements, however, came from groups of as few as two animals.

The brains of exposed mice also contained higher levels of several chemicals involved in inflammation.

Whether the inflammation damaged blood vessels or whether other processes contributed to both problems remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that within the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, lies a smaller area called the dentate gyrus. New brain cells continue to form there after birth in mice.

Interestingly, pollution did not significantly affect how many new cells ordinary mice produced. The problem was keeping those cells alive, as fewer survived over a period of 30 days.

In mice prone to Alzheimer’s disease, both the production and survival of upcoming cells suffered.

Pollution also disturbed the balance between two forms of a molecule called NAD, which cells depend on for energy production and processes involved in repairing damage.

In a recent development, much of the investigation centered on microglia, the immune cells that live inside the brain. Sanjay Rajagopalan, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, co-led the work.

“By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” said Sanjay Rajagopalan.

When the researchers compared polluted-air and filtered-air groups, they identified changes in the activity of 766 genes in ordinary mice. They also found that genetic background influenced how 2,876 genes responded to pollution.

“These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it,” Rajagopalan noted.

Alzheimer’s disease is associated with the accumulation of a protein called amyloid in the brain. As the protein collects, it forms deposits known as plaques.

Despite examining brain tissue with two different staining methods, the team could not find these plaques in ordinary mice that had breathed polluted air. Their memory problems had developed without detectable amyloid buildup.

Andrew Pieper, a professor of translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, was also a senior author.

“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” remarked Andrew Pieper.

According to recent reports, how much pollution each person actually breathed remains unknown. The team estimated exposure using home addresses.

Only white participants and male mice were studied. Gene analysis involved just three mice per group.

Sources indicate that “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors,” Pieper stated.

Air pollution’s role in human dementia needs further investigation. But unlike inherited risk, pollution can be reduced.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation.

#191682. Rainbow trout faced a familiar virus, but tiny plastic fibers changed their chances of survival

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (999 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Rainbow trout faced a familiar virus, but tiny plastic fibers changed their chances of survival

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.
  • Microplastics come in many shapes, and a new study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.
  • In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.

Microplastics come in many shapes, and a new study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.

In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.

Trout that lived with round nylon particles of similar width fared no worse than fish with no plastic at all.

The fibers didn’t kill fish on their own. Without the virus, plastic of either shape made no difference to survival.

The study came from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science at William & Mary, where Meredith Evans Seeley, Robert Hale and Andrew Wargo work. Anna Mehlhorn, an undergraduate at the time, is now at Cornell.

“Not all plastics are created equal, and so that creates an opportunity to identify the worst forms of pollution and come up with solutions,” Wargo said.

Three years ago, the same group reported that microplastics made a trout virus deadlier. Nylon microfibers stood out: in that earlier work, fish exposed to them faced a hazard of death 6.4 times that of fish given the virus alone.

“We saw the effect with the nylon fibers and had to ask, ‘Is it the fact it’s a fiber or is it the fact that it was nylon?'” Hale remarked.

To answer that, the team kept the material the same and changed the shape. The fibers were about 0.02 inches (500 micrometers) long and 10 micrometers wide, the kind that shed from synthetic fabric.

The powder was made of rounded nylon grains averaging 15 to 20 micrometers across, about as wide as the fibers but nowhere near as long.

The team raised 800 juvenile rainbow trout in 40 tanks of 20 fish each. Every other day, the plastic groups got a dose of fibers or powder in their water, and the tank sat still for a day before it was flushed.

Most groups got plastic for the full eight weeks; two fiber groups got it only in the first or last four.

Halfway through, half the tanks were dosed with infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus, a major cause of losses on trout farms.

Fish started dying a few days later, and the dying largely ended within about two weeks.

It has been revealed that by the end, 39% of the trout exposed to both the virus and eight weeks of fibers were alive. In tanks that got the virus with no plastic, 56% survived, and in tanks with neither, 86% did.

In the statistical model, eight weeks of fibers raised the odds of death 2.03 times compared with no particles.

None of the other plastic treatments had a significant effect, including the round powder for eight weeks and the fibers given only before or only after the virus.

The team also sampled tank water every few days to measure how much virus the fish were shedding. Shedding peaked three days after the virus went in and fell to undetectable levels by day 47 in every treatment.

The plastic groups did not differ, though the eight-week fiber tanks showed a trend toward the highest peaks.

Recent findings suggest that the authors wrote that measuring shedding from groups of fish in only four tanks per treatment may have limited the study’s power. A few super-shedders could mask the rest.

It has been revealed that so the fibers did not seem to make the virus more abundant. They seemed to make the fish easier to infect.

The researchers suspect the long, stiff fibers damage protective tissue such as the gills, which they described in the university’s account as the fibers’ pokiness.

“It’s likely creating an easier path for that virus to infect that host,” Seeley said.

It has been revealed that if microplastic fibers open a door for the virus, the damage has to be there before the virus arrives, and it probably has to keep up afterward. That is what the tanks indicated.

It has been revealed that fibers given only after infection did about as well as no plastic. Fibers given only before the virus pushed mortality up toward the chronic group’s level, but the difference was not significant.

The authors pointed to tissue damage from plastic in other animals. In seabirds, scarring from swallowed plastic has been given its own name, plasticosis. Inflammation from microplastics is also under study in fish and in human tissue.

“One of the things that was becoming clear to us is that microplastics have really significant impacts, but they’re not always lethal,” Seeley said.

The team used one high concentration of plastic, 10 milligrams per liter, to make the effect easy to see. The authors wrote that future work should test a range of doses to find the levels that matter in real water.

The fibers and the powder were also not chemically identical, since the fibers were a stiffer grade of nylon.

The work was funded by the NOAA Marine Debris Program. The group is now working with a commercial trout farm to find out which microplastics turn up in working tanks and where they come from.

Trout farms use nylon line and other plastic gear that can break down into microplastics, and the particles are also common in the water where wild fish live.

Earlier work has shown that microplastics can carry microbes and change how pathogens behave.

According to recent reports, people are also exposed to microplastic fibers through indoor dust. The authors wrote that the results call for research into whether microplastics change the course of infectious disease in wildlife and people.

They also want to know which features of a particle, such as rigidity and length, do the damage.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Industry observers note that house and Senate Republicans picked their fresh campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you.
  • In a recent development, the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived.
  • Kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you. But futurist Ray Kurzweil thinks modern medicine might be on the cusp of changing that, possibly as soon as 2029.

In a recent development, the advances are arriving fast enough, he indicates, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived. After that, he predicts, it’s possible that we’ll all start actually gaining time.

Kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards. But your expected remaining years of life would go in the opposite direction, getting longer with each passing year as medical interventions improved.

Our earlier coverage took a closer look at that prediction and Kurzweil’s argument about how accelerating medical advances could get us there. S. Jay Olshansky, a professor emeritus of epidemiology and public health at the University of Illinois Chicago, has a less enthusiastic name for it.

“I refer to LEV as voodoo demography,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

In a recent development, yet Olshansky thinks research into slowing aging could produce important benefits, too. His objection concerns the much bigger promise that those benefits will keep arriving fast enough to outrun aging itself.

Industry observers note that life expectancy describes a population, while lifespan is how long an individual actually lives. To determine life expectancy, researchers calculate how many people die at certain ages and come up with statistical predictions. Plenty of people will live longer, and plenty will die sooner.

Industry observers note that that distinction matters when somebody promises to add years to your life. The Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table, for instance, gives a 60-year-old man 21.79 remaining years and a 61-year-old man 21.04. Both calculations assume that 2023 death rates continue throughout the rest of their lives. They illustrate how expected remaining years generally shrink with age under fixed conditions.

It has been revealed that kurzweil’s prediction depends on medicine improving fast enough to beat those numbers, and to keep beating them every year. Imagine a 60-year-old who is expected to live about 22 more years. If treatments got better swiftly enough, that person could turn 61 and find they now had 23 years ahead instead of fewer. That would be an impressive gain. But one year of progress wouldn’t be escape velocity. To stay ahead of aging, medicine would have to do the same thing the next year, and every year after that. Without that continuous progress, it’s just wishful thinking.

Recent findings suggest that olshansky wants to know what evidence would convince Kurzweil’s supporters that humanity had actually reached escape velocity. Beating one disease wouldn’t be enough. A treatment might save someone from one illness and give them more years, but another illness could still cut that life short.

Olshansky does see reason for hope in aging research. He notes work underway “likely will yield reductions in the rate of biological aging.” That could mean people develop age-related illnesses later in life than they would otherwise, giving them more years in good health.

Sources indicate that olshansky would look at whether a treatment changed people’s chances of dying as they got older. Do illnesses show up later, and do people really survive longer? “It’s important that total mortality be the measurable endpoint,” he says. A treatment might prevent a heart attack, but that wouldn’t protect a patient from dying later from cancer. Researchers would have to count deaths from all causes to see whether a given treatment actually bought people more time.

Recent findings suggest that suppose a treatment delayed several illnesses and helped recipients live longer. That could change how people planned their later years, even if medicine never caught up with aging. People could have more good years after they stopped working, and some might choose to stay on the job longer. Before making those plans, people would need to know how much longer the treatment could keep them alive and well.

Sources indicate that for now, gains in life expectancy have been getting harder to come by. In a 2024 study in Nature Aging, Olshansky and his colleagues analyzed the death rates between 1990 and 2019 in places where people live the longest, as well as in the United States. Life expectancy was still generally growing, but the pace of that growth had slowed.

Olshansky explains that much of the major rise in life expectancy in the past came from keeping children alive and preventing mothers from dying in childbirth. Saving a child’s life can add decades to a population’s average life expectancy. But in countries where most people already live into their 70s and 80s, those gains have mostly been made. The remaining deaths happen mainly among older people, and saving an 85-year-old from one illness adds far fewer years. That’s why it’s vital to slow down aging. If researchers could slow the biological process behind many diseases of old age, life expectancy might start rising faster again. That possibility, Olshansky notes, is what makes the research worth pursuing.

Recent findings suggest that if only a few people received an anti-aging treatment, the country’s life expectancy wouldn’t change, Olshansky says. To find out whether the treatment works, researchers would have to follow the people who took it and compare how long they survive with similar people who didn’t.

And the only way to confirm a promise of 20 extra years is to watch people live them. “A specific prediction of a numerical gain in either life expectancy or lifespan associated with an intervention would require an observed gain of the predicted amount,” he states. Encouraging early results could justify more research, but they couldn’t show how much time a treatment added. Scientists could have good news in 2029 and still need decades to learn how many years people actually gained.

Even then, one success wouldn’t mean we’d reached escape velocity. Kurzweil’s prediction needs each advance to arrive in time to add more years, then another advance to do the same, and another after that. Kurzweil has noted that people could still die even if medicine delivered the gains he predicts. Olshansky’s worry is that grand promises could overshadow the research he’s most hopeful about: work that could actually slow aging.

Slowing aging alone would give people plenty to look forward to, deadline or not: more years, and the health to enjoy them. Finding out how many years would take patience, because the people in those studies would still be busy living.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a newly introduced world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer notes. “You have to really be curious.”.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

It has been revealed that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer notes it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he notes. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

Recent findings suggest that the phases of the Moon are: Upcoming Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the latest antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Recent findings suggest that black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four Fresh Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

Sources indicate that how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and Fresh Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

  • In a recent development, the arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability.
  • Now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs.
  • “AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr said in his speech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability. Since ChatGPT brought large language models (LLMs) into the mainstream in late 2022, instability in the job market has been a given. As the technology has required more and more resources, instability in utilities’ ability to supply power also became painfully clear. And as AI companies’ valuations skyrocketed in recent years, worries of an AI bubble have highlighted the instability of millions of retirement plans.

Now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs. In a speech in Milan last week, Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr warned that AI’s ability to react to a financial crisis at unprecedented speed could make future runs far more devastating.

“AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr said in his speech. “Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.”.

Bank runs have been a fixture of U.S. financial crises since the Panic of 1792, when the newly independent country’s government was a whopping three years old. Banks don’t keep enough cash on hand to cover every deposit, but instead use that cash for loans and investments. But if the job or stock market takes a turn for the worse, customers might attempt to withdraw funds all at once, forcing banks to sell off investments at a loss, pushing them toward insolvency. After widespread bank failures during the Great Depression, the U.S. government created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to protect depositors. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, serves as lender of last resort, providing emergency loans to banks experiencing runs.

It has been revealed that these failsafes have typically operated at the speed of a human. But in a world where AI can pour gasoline on a financial panic by accelerating withdrawals upon detecting telltale instability in markets, bank runs could unfold in mere minutes.

And that isn’t the only concern AI presents to the banking world. Bank executives told Axios in late October that banks are struggling to distinguish between AI bots and human users, prompting them to restrict third-party AI access to their platforms. Major banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, and Bank of America have already done so.

Sources indicate that “We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorize money moving out of your account,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC last month. “We’re working with the agentic agent providers to say, ‘Hey, you really don’t want consumers coming back and say money moved over from my account and I don’t know why and I don’t know where it went and the agent did it.’”.

In a recent development, the swift efficiency of AI agents, tasked with squeezing every possible cent from a customer’s money, means they could also move money from non-interest-bearing deposits (such as a checking account) into high-yield accounts paying upwards of 5 percent. The problem is that banks rely on low-interest accounts to fund loans, so a sudden exodus would inject unwanted volatility into the financial system.

  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

In 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a latest observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

In a recent development, on Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#191672. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1378 w)

Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming latest stars.
  • But ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • In a recent development, now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming latest stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

But ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

In a recent development, now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

Industry observers note that in order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

In a recent development, such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that highlights what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Major Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations indicated a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

Industry observers note that but to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies says, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

Industry observers note that first, Davies’ team measured how many latest stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how promptly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

The researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

Industry observers note that the verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies stated in a press release.

Sources indicate that finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies notes. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

The speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, notes Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Sources indicate that davies indicates that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies indicates. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really crucial for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

The case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

In a recent development, shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they indicated up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Industry observers note that despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

It has been revealed that overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

Industry observers note that in the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

In a recent development, according to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top concern concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent noted it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent remarked his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Sources indicate that neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls indicated that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Sources indicate that independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

It has been revealed that at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent remarked the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

It has been revealed that democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

Industry observers note that david Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and latest.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

According to recent reports, most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo claims. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (396 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that even the best-laid plans can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that even the best-laid plans can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

In a recent development, he named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” indicates Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.
