Best Things to Do in Hamilton, Ontario

📅 14 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us.
  • Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.
  • Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something fresh therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something new therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

Hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

Industry observers note that the house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a substantial museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

It has been revealed that HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Industry observers note that known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

In a recent development, dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how notable the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

It has been revealed that the Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Recent findings suggest that dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Industry observers note that hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:.

In a recent development, webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

According to recent reports, important Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

According to recent reports, dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

Spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Estimated reading time: 19 minutes.

In a recent development, dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

Industry observers note that the Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

According to recent reports, dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

Industry observers note that hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

In a recent development, hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

Recent findings suggest that the Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a major part of the city’s story.

ThGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

The Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

Recent findings suggest that hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Sources indicate that held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of event that shows how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Recent findings suggest that dave & Deb’s Tip: Plan your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

Industry observers note that the Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most key artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

It has been revealed that hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre company and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

📅 18 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured.
  • Industry observers note that the travel insurance organization Safety Wing is looking to change that.
  • I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just rolled out what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health blueprint, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

Industry observers note that the travel insurance organization Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just rolled out what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really swiftly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

It has been revealed that I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

In a recent development, for those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

It has been revealed that visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

It has been revealed that I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

  • Recent findings suggest that most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

We’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but big on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend aims in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Recent findings suggest that dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the big roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

According to recent reports, canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

In a recent development, this is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines promptly.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Industry observers note that kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

According to recent reports, the waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

It has been revealed that caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

It has been revealed that dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

After the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Sources indicate that stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

According to recent reports, this is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

In a recent development, dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Industry observers note that paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

It has been revealed that best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Sources indicate that kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

Recent findings suggest that st. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

This is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole initiative.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Industry observers note that peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

The Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

Industry observers note that this is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Sources indicate that dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Sources indicate that dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Recent findings suggest that prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and substantial nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Recent findings suggest that algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the plan simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

You won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Sources indicate that dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

In a recent development, QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Sources indicate that A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

In a recent development, before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

Sources indicate that you may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

It has been revealed that do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

In a recent development, if the message states you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Industry observers note that most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Recent findings suggest that do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

In a recent development, open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car organization, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

In a recent development, first, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

If you scanned a suspicious code:.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

Industry observers note that but now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

Recent findings suggest that the trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

Sources indicate that as an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, former Rep.
  • In a recent development, former Rep.
  • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott revealed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

It has been revealed that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against fresh sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

It has been revealed that as he mentioned, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he stated in a statement at the time.

It has been revealed that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

In a recent development, “Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

My First “Fresh” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card.
  • It has been revealed that the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards.
  • Recent findings suggest that well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the newly introduced changes.

It has been revealed that the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

But what about the redemption of points?

Recent findings suggest that well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

It has been revealed that chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the notable bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a fresh “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Sources indicate that previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the fresh version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

According to recent reports, typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

Recent findings suggest that BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive….

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

Industry observers note that you can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Latest Update: A Guide to NYC’s Little Italy—and the Culinary Gems Hidden Among the Tourist Traps

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in New York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike.
  • According to recent reports, A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings.
  • Located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in New York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike. Sandwiched between SoHo and the Lower East Side, this jewel box area is home to long-standing, family-owned restaurants and authentic Italian bakeries, the majority of which have been neighborhood staples for decades. Yet despite its touristy atmosphere, a unique feeling of old school New York magic hangs in the air; beyond the personality-less stands and souvenir shops, framed family photos on restaurant walls and structural imperfections of tenement buildings speak to a bygone area of the city’s past, evoking a sense of nostalgia that so many neighborhoods lack. Pop down to Mulberry Street and see for yourself—though be sure you know which spots are actually legit (that’s where we come in).

According to recent reports, A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings. While the southern and western boundaries of Canal Street and Lafayette Streets remain unchanged, the historic easterly Bowery boundary has arguably shifted to Elizabeth Street; similarly, the northerly boundary of Kenmare has also condensed down, according to many, to Broome Street. For the sake of this piece, we’re using the boundaries of Lafayette Street, Canal Street, Elizabeth Street, and Broome Street as a happy medium.

Located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams. The restaurant quickly garnered attention shortly after opening in 1972, when mobster Joe "Crazy Joe" Gallo was shot in the restaurant’s dining room. Like its mafia-related history, the food at Umberto’s is as Italian-American as it gets. Baked clams and fried calamari are the appetizer list’s biggest show-stoppers, while superbly chilled clams on the half-shell pair exquisitely with equally cold (and generously sized) cocktails from the bar. Seafood-focused mains are the name of the game here, including the garlicky linguini and clam sauce and recently resurfaced scungilli with pasta served with piping hot red sauce.

Address: 132 Mulberry Street, Upcoming York, NY 10013.

For Italian-American eats in a less stereotypically Little Italy ambiance, Il Cortile is the way to go. Contrary to the old school Italian vibes found in the majority of the neighborhood’s restaurants, Il Cortile’s atrium-style glass ceiling and plant-filled room feel more like dining al fresco in Trastevere than the heart of Mulberry Street. The family-owned restaurant’s neighborhood roots date back to 1975, with a solid focus on Northern Italian cuisine. The homemade cheese ravioli and wood-fired pizzas are always a safe bet, though for meat lovers, springing for the Fettuccine di Parma made with sweet sausage and wild mushrooms won’t disappoint—and be sure to save room for the pillowy soft tiramisu made with creamy mascarpone and imported Italian ladyfingers drenched in espresso.

Address: 125 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013.

Original Vincent’s, often called The Original Vincent’s Clam Bar, is home to one of the richest restaurant success stories in Little Italy. Founded in 1904 by Giuseppe and Carmela Siano, the business began as a sidewalk street cart serving up fresh seafood and jars of homemade red sauce, available in mild, medium, and hot. Today, the restaurant sits on the corner of Mott and Hester Streets, and is still known for its signature gravies, baked clams, and linguini-based pasta dishes (don’t skip the frutti di mare). As in its earliest days, Original Vincent’s still sells jars of their red sauce to-go, making replicating the restaurant’s pasta dishes at home a breeze—simply grab a bottle of Chianti, cue up your Louis Primo playlist and voila.

Address: 119 Mott St, Upcoming York, NY 10013.

Paesano of Mulberry Street is home to one of the coziest interiors in Little Italy, offering a peaceful refuge from the neighborhood bustle. Rustic twig bunches and leafy plants strung with twinkle lights hang from the ceiling, while traditional Italian frescos and framed family photographs adorn the whitewashed brick walls. Originally opened in 1961, the restaurant remains owned by the same family and continues to be known for their Southern Italian recipes, including linguini with clam sauce, wood-fired pizzas, and savory chicken marsala drenched in sautéed mushrooms. Meat lovers, don’t skip the restaurant’s signature Veal A La Paesano, featuring a juicy and tender veal base layered with thin slices of prosciutto, steamed broccoli, and gooey mozzarella cheese finished with succulent brown gravy.

Address: 136 Mulberry St, Upcoming York, NY 10013.

According to recent reports, for serious pizza lovers, a trip to Lombardi’s is a no-brainer. Tucked on the corner of Mott and Spring, this neighborhood institution is credited as America’s first pizzeria, originally founded by Gennaro Lombardi in 1905. Lombardi swiftly rose to fame for his large, heavily-topped pies, which he baked in an on-site, coal-and-gas oven. The result? Smoky crusts topped with perfectly balanced tomato sauce and gobs of whole milk mozzarella—along with sweet Italian sausage and various other accoutrements. The interior oozes with classic Newly introduced York charm, featuring tables clad in red-and-white checkered cloths and framed family photographs strung along the red-hued walls. Head’s up, the spot is cash only, and while there’s an ATM on site, we recommend coming prepared to avoid the withdrawal fee.

Address: 30 Spring St, New York, NY 10012.

Pasquale Jones-12_2. Brussels Sprout Pizza with Red Onion, Smoked Mozzarella & Lemon.

In a sea of mediocre neighborhood wine lists, Pasqule Jones offers a breath of fresh air for Little Italy exploring wine lovers. Situated on the cusp of the neighborhood’s boundaries (and easily identifiable by its rainbow neon lights), this Italian-American pizzeria first opened its doors in 2016 and swiftly became a staple for industry folks and visiting oenophiles alike. Beloved for its wood-fired New York style pizzas (don’t miss the signature clam pie) and thick, homemade pastas, the restaurant’s warm-yet-casual ambiance is ideal for posting up with a pie and a bottle—especially if you’re after great Burgundy, Champagne, or Italian reds. Expect classic picks from Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Domaine de l’Arlot, and Vietti, as well ample fun and fresh selections from Sandlands, Chacra, and Domaine Gramenon.

Address: 187 Mulberry St, Upcoming York, NY 10012.

Address: 195 Grand St, New York, NY 10013.

Although less famous than nearby Ferrara, Caffé Palermo features the innate Italian charm one looks for when wandering the neighborhood. Owned and operated by Baby John DeLutro (the self-proclaimed “Cannoli King”) since 1973, the establishment lives up to its owner’s moniker, offering flavored iterations—including pistachio and hazelnut made with sweet ricotta cream, the former of which is one of the joint’s standouts—in perfectly crisp shells. What Palermo does have over Ferrara is a solid amount of outdoor seating, ideal for posting up with a cappuccino and people watching on Mulberry.

Address: 148 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013.

La Compagnie des Vins Surnaturels.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a wine break between pizza and pastries, this is just the ticket. Located on Little Italy's western limits (Centre Street between Broome and Grand), this French-inspired wine bar offers extensive by-the-glass options and shareable bites, including cheese and charcuterie boards to larger main courses, including beef tartare and lemon spaghetti. The comprehensive wine list, which features anywhere from 750 to 1,000+ references at all times, leans unsurprisingly French, though ample selections from Italy, Spain, and the USA are also available. Our suggestion? Post up with a bottle of Grower Champagne and relish in the perfectly executed Parisian bar à vin ambiance.

Address: 249 Centre St, Fresh York, NY 10013.

Address: 409 Broome St, Newly introduced York, NY 10013.

According to recent reports, technically located on the cusp of Little Italy’s historic boundaries (Kenmare and Broome Streets), La Esquina offers a flavor-packed reprieve from the classic red-sauce joints synonymous with the neighborhood. Situated in a former counter deli, this multi-level Mexican hotspot is best known for its casual taqueria (located in ‘The Corner Deli’ space) serving tacos, tortas, and ceviche. However, for those looking for something a bit stronger, head through the secret door and down the stairs to find the restaurant’s underground speakeasy. Lit by candle and adorned with Lucha Libre posters, the bar’s high-energy ambiance is prime for enjoying queso fundido and smoky Mexican street corn (elotes callejeros) washed down with expertly crafted agave-based cocktails.

Address: 114 Kenmare St, Newly introduced York, NY 10012.

#191536. Latest Update: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Latest Update: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the challenges were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin noted “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

Recent findings suggest that “This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin stated the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

In a recent development, “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin stated. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

It has been revealed that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

According to recent reports, the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority remarked Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology challenges related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and noted their committee would “thoroughly review the challenges that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At matter in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have noted they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally rolled out a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are at the moment scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen remarked Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A newly introduced issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

Recent findings suggest that "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy stated in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

Sources indicate that on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

According to recent reports, that includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is presently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.
